b: A medical practice evolves over time. Over three decades, I have seen my patient population change, the relationships with my patients change, and the common causes of death change. Even what I enjoy most about my work has changed.

I didn’t foresee any of these changes because, at no time in my 30s or 40s, did I think about what my practice would look like in my dotage. That said, none of these changes are terribly surprising. What has surprised me is how an aging patient panel affects clinical reasoning.

Being a good, well-calibrated, primary care doctor means understanding that most people who see you have nothing wrong with them. This is a total exaggeration and sounds kind of dismissive. What I mean is that most concerns that patients present are not related to the development of a new life-altering or life-shortening disease. Most things people come to primary care doctors for are passing symptoms of the human condition. To paraphrase Voltaire, a good primary care doctor orders few tests, avoids doing harm, and amuses the patient while nature (maybe with a little help from modern medicine) cures the disease.

Of course, I am not at all discounting the value of primary care doctors. I am proud to be one. To prove my bona fides (and shamelessly self-promote), here are Sensible Medicine essays that I have written defending and promoting my kind.
A Heartfelt Plea to Become A Primary Care General Internist
What Kind of Doctor Are You?
Seven Things I Love about Being a General Internist

At some point, a primary care practice reaches a tipping point. This might happen when the doctor reaches a certain age, when the average age of the patients passes the population's average life expectancy, or when Saturn completes a revolution. At this time, the doctor needs to recalibrate, to recognize that many symptoms are signs of something serious. The doctor also needs to acknowledge that aging brings more symptoms, many of which don’t need evaluation.

Eventually, we all receive a diagnosis that will be our undoing. We become aware of the diagnosis abruptly — a finding on a CT, an acute MI, a fall with a hip fracture — or gradually — increasing forgetfulness, the slow descent into frailty, the gnawing abdominal pain. Sometimes the terminal diagnosis is made by the patient, sometimes by an emergency room doctor, and usually — for those fortunate to have one — by a primary care doctor.

As a patient population ages, the primary care doctor spends more time making these diagnoses. Added to the benign back pain, seasonal allergies, and eczema are new diagnoses of Alzheimer’s, pancreatic cancer, and interstitial lung disease. At this point, the certainty with which the doctor could say, “This is nothing, don’t worry about it, we don’t need to do a test,” is, well, tested. The pretest probability of disease increases, and more symptoms cross the test threshold.
People have a lot of concerns

At the same time that more symptoms are caused by serious disease, there are more symptoms. They say that “nobody gets out of here alive”. They also say that “old age is not for wimps”. As we age, we live with more aches, more pains, and more disability.

For the doctor, both the numerator — the symptoms caused by serious disease — and the denominator — that total number of symptoms — increase. There are more needles in the haystack, but the haystack is also bigger.

This means that the primary care doctor needs to recalibrate, to understand the relationship between her diagnostic accuracy and her confidence in that accuracy. She needs to rely on clinical acumen, whether that means pulling the trigger on a work-up or re-engaging the safety.
Not every illness should be treated

The third complexity is that in older populations, more symptoms should be left unevaluated and untreated. A lumbar spine MRI that shows spinal stenosis might be important at 65, less so at 85. A coronary artery calcium score over 300 might change management and outcomes at 50; it will not at 80.

Acknowledging this reality and incorporating it into visits takes time, one of the many things primary care doctors don’t have. It is so much easier to order a test (or write a prescription, or make a referral) than it is to discuss why the best action is inaction.
I’m going for humor, making this a separate section. There is no simple, pithy wrap-up.

Primary care medicine is hard. I don’t think it gets harder as your population ages; it just gets hard in a different way. In the early years, clinical excellence means trusting your feel for prevalence, caring for people appropriately, and making them better without medicalizing every symptom. In the later years, excellence means recognizing that every symptom might be the beginning of the end while still managing those symptoms with wisdom and parsimony.
